newsitem.title: FRANCE: Polish president says Russian fears on NATO to fade.
newsitem.headline: Polish president says Russian fears on NATO to fade.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Wednesday Russian fears about the admission of its former East European satellites into NATO would fade like fears which initially surrounded German unification.

"I remember all the fears connected with German reunification, the fears of a Germanisation of Europe, fears also shared by public opinion in Poland and in France," he told the Western European Union's (WEU) parliamentary assembly.

"There were lots of fears but after reunification (in 1990), we can say that with a united Germany, Europe and the world are more secure, more stable and more cooperative place. I am sure this will also be true and repeat itself after the enlargement of NATO (to former Warsaw Pact states), he said.
Kwasniewski insisted that Poland's desire to join NATO had nothing to do with fear of Russia, indicating that his country felt more uneasy about events in neighbouring troubled Belarus.
"We are sure that Russia can have good relations with NATO. Russia and Ukraine should have special treaties with an enlarged NATO," he said.

Kwasniewski, in a prepared speech followed by parliamentarians' questions and a separate news conference, was careful not to offend any side in a tug-of-war between the United States and France over the existence of a European pillar within NATO.

Under French instigation, the 1991 Maastricht Treaty designated the 10-nation WEU as the future defence arm of the European Union, but Britain has since opposed bringing the defence grouping under the authority of the EU's summit of heads of state and government.

The Polish president, saying his country wanted to join NATO and WEU at the earliest possible date, said Warsaw believed "the community of interests between Europe and the United States is a fact of life."
"Europe continuously needs the engagement of the United States just as the U.S. requires European support," he said.
Kwasniewski praised the concept of a European pillar inside NATO and said Poland was willing to operate with other European states in actions in which the United States did not take part.
But he said "the European defence entity...must not be perceived as NATO's substitute or rival but a complementary and supportive organisation."

The Polish leader said a Tuesday bombing in a Paris commuter railway train, which he presumed was by Islamic fundamentalists, was a problem which should be seen as a challenge for all European states.
